prompt.system:
You merge three profiles of the same prize-committee member into one integrated profile. Three different language
models (A, O and G) wrote them independently from their own knowledge, without web access, so each profile can
contain errors, gaps or outdated information.

- Use only what the three profiles say. Do not add facts, works, years, coauthors or roles from your own knowledge.
- For every field, interest and work, list in "support" the letters of the profiles that state it (A, O, G). Merge
  entries that describe the same thing (the same work under slightly different titles, the same field in other
  words); keep the title, year and venue that most profiles agree on.
- Where the profiles disagree on a detail (a year, a venue, a coauthor, a role), keep the better-supported version and
  describe the disagreement in that entry's "conflict" and in "disagreements"; otherwise "conflict" is "".
- Keep entries that only one profile states, with that single letter. Drop an entry only if it clearly belongs to a
  different person (a namesake) or contradicts the member's affiliation, and say so in "caveats".
- Write the integrated persona from what the profiles share; where they diverge, keep the better-supported view and
  name the alternative in "support_note". Keep the persona grounded in the record; do not predict whom the member
  will support for the 2026 prize.
- "caveats": what a reader should check before relying on the profile (single-profile or low-confidence items,
  knowledge cutoffs, possible namesakes, a profile that did not recognize the person).

identity.name: Kerstin Enflo
identity.affiliation: Department of Economic History, Lund University
identity.note: All three profiles recognize her as a professor of economic history at Lund University. They describe her as a quantitative economic historian working on Swedish and European long-run regional growth, regional inequality and convergence, and historical national and regional accounts (regional GDP estimation). Profile A adds technology (electrification) and labour. Profiles O and G add economic geography and transport infrastructure. Confidence in the identification varies: A rates it medium, O and G high. A explicitly knows of no namesake in economics. She is listed as a co-opted member of the 2026 Economic Sciences Prize Committee.

fields.field: Economic history, quantitative / cliometric (Swedish, Nordic and European long-run development)
fields.note: All three profiles list this as a core field. JEL codes are the union across profiles: N33/N34 come from A only and N73 from G only.

fields.field: Regional economics and economic geography: regional growth, convergence/divergence, spatial inequality, urbanization
fields.note: A frames it as regional growth, inequality and convergence. O adds economic geography and urbanization. G labels it Regional and Urban Economics. O47 is from A only and R40 from G only.

fields.field: Historical national and regional accounts (quantitative reconstruction of regional GDP and long-run data series)
fields.note: G frames this more broadly as 'Macroeconomics and National Accounts' (E01, medium confidence). N10 is from O only.

fields.field: Structural change and long-run development (Nordic and European)
fields.note: A lists it as a separate field. O folds structural change into a broader field covering infrastructure, market integration, migration and regional adjustment. O52 is from A only.

fields.field: Infrastructure, transport, market integration, migration and regional adjustment in industrialization
fields.note: O lists this as a field at medium confidence. G supports the transport-infrastructure theme through its recent interests and its railway paper, and uses N73/R40 in its other fields.

fields.field: Technology diffusion, electrification and labour relations in history
fields.note: Only A lists this (medium confidence). It is tied to A's electrification and labour-conflict paper.

recent_interests.topic: Long-run regional inequality, growth and spatial divergence in Sweden and Europe across industrialization and the twentieth century
recent_interests.period: c. 2019–2024 (O); G gives the historical period studied (late 19th century to modern era) rather than a research period
recent_interests.note: Both rate this high confidence. They present it as a continuation of her regional GDP and regional inequality agenda.

recent_interests.topic: Construction of historical regional GDP, economic geography and other long-run quantitative datasets, including European regional GDP databases
recent_interests.note: A specifically mentions Nordic/Swedish contributions to the Rosés–Wolf European regional GDP project. O and G describe data construction in general terms.

recent_interests.topic: Transport infrastructure, railways, market integration and spatial development in historical Sweden
recent_interests.period: c. 2019–2024 (O); 19th and 20th centuries as the period studied (G)
recent_interests.note: G cites railway-expansion studies at high confidence. O rates this medium and is unsure about specific post-2019 publications.

recent_interests.topic: Roles of structural change, migration, urbanization and policy in mitigating regional inequality
recent_interests.note: O infers this from her 1860–2000 work on Swedish regional inequality (medium confidence).
A attributes this to joint work with Anna Missiaia (medium confidence).

recent_interests.topic: Electrification and its effects on labour markets, labour conflict and political mobilization in Sweden
recent_interests.note: A attributes this to work with Jakob Molinder and Tobias Karlsson using Swedish grid expansion (medium confidence).

recent_interests.topic: Historical roots of democratization, state capacity and political change in Sweden using micro/parish-level data
recent_interests.note: A gives this low confidence and calls it a general impression with uncertain specifics.

representative_works.title: Swedish regional GDP 1855–2000: Estimations and general trends in the Swedish regional system
representative_works.contribution: Constructs long-run county-level GDP for Sweden. It documents regional convergence and divergence over industrialization and gives a baseline for long-run spatial analysis.

representative_works.title: Coping with regional inequality in Sweden: structural change, migrations, and policy, 1860–2000
representative_works.contribution: Explains the evolution of Swedish regional inequality and convergence through structural change and internal migration. It also assesses the role of policy; G specifies active labour market policies.

representative_works.title: Regional GDP estimates for Sweden, 1571–1850
representative_works.contribution: Extends Swedish regional output estimates back into the early modern period, before modern national accounts. This enables analysis of spatial development over several centuries.
representative_works.conflict: The profiles agree on the title but not the details. A gives 2018, Historical Methods, with Anna Missiaia. O gives 2011, Economic History Review, with Johan Söderberg. Neither version has majority support. A's version is kept because it is consistent with A's other Missiaia work, but this is unresolved and should be verified.

representative_works.title: Locomotives of local growth: The short- and long-term impact of state-owned railways in Sweden
representative_works.contribution: Estimates the causal impact of 19th-century state railway expansion on urban growth and local development in Sweden using a quasi-experimental design.

representative_works.title: Between Malthus and the industrial take-off: regional inequality in Sweden, 1571–1850
representative_works.contribution: Analyses the dynamics and drivers of pre-industrial regional inequality in Sweden.

representative_works.title: More power to the people: electricity adoption, technological change, and labor conflict
representative_works.contribution: Uses the staggered rollout of electricity in Sweden to show how technology adoption affected strikes and labour conflict.

persona.summary: A quantitative economic historian at Lund focused on long-run, spatially disaggregated development: regional growth, regional inequality and convergence, and structural change. Her work is built on painstaking construction of historical regional GDP and other datasets. She bridges economic history with mainstream, especially regional and urban, economics. The persona is inferred from her research record, not from known private views.
persona.research_lens: Development over long horizons and across space. She asks how structural change, migration, infrastructure and technology shape regional disparities and long-term growth. She also asks whether a contribution's insights hold up across historical periods and contexts rather than only in a narrow modern setting.
persona.methods_and_evidence: Three elements recur across the profiles. First, construction of historical regional accounts and archival or statistical datasets. Second, long-run descriptive accounting and decomposition of inequality. Third, quasi-experimental or microeconometric identification using historical variation, such as staggered rollout of railways or the electricity grid, difference-in-differences and instrumental variables. representative_works.title: Between Malthus and the industrial take-off: regional inequality in Sweden, 1571–1850

representative_works.title: More power to the people: electricity adoption, technological change, and labor conflict
representative_works.contribution: Uses the staggered rollout of electricity in Sweden to show how technology adoption affected strikes and labour conflict.

A.persona_summary: A Lund-trained quantitative economic historian in the Scandinavian tradition of historical national accounts associated with Lennart Schön. Her work combines careful construction of long-run data with modern causal identification, applied to regional development, structural change, technology and labour.
A.identity_note: Kerstin Enflo is an economic historian at the Department of Economic History, Lund University. She is known mainly for quantitative work on Swedish and European regional development: historical regional GDP estimation, regional inequality and convergence, structural change, and the economic history of technology (electrification) and labour. I am not aware of a namesake in economics. Details of her career and committee service are less certain than her main research lines.
A.knowledge_limits: My knowledge comes from training data running roughly to 2024–2025. I am fairly confident about her regional GDP and regional inequality work. I am less confident about exact titles, years and coauthors beyond the core papers, about her most recent projects, about her editorial and administrative roles, and about the start and scope of her Nobel committee work. I have no information on her deliberations or preferences regarding the 2026 prize.
